title: Mandate and the Hashemite Kingdom
subtitle: 1914–1958 · The British Conquest, the 1920 Revolt, an Imported King and an Invented State — Kirkuk Oil, the Farhud and the End of Jewish Iraq, the Failed Liberal Experiment, and the 14 July Revolution

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The conquest and the Mandate, Faisal I and the founding of the Kingdom, Ghazi and the boy-king, Nuri al-Saʿid and the old regime, the army and the coups, the Rashid Ali affair, the opposition parties, and the 14 July Revolution

entries.label: The conquest and the Mandate
entries.hint: Britain took Iraq in a hard campaign — the surrender at Kut, the fall of Baghdad in 1917, Mosul grabbed at the armistice — and was handed it as a League of Nations Mandate at San Remo in 1920. The Cairo Conference of 1921 fixed the design: an Arab kingdom under a Hashemite king, run indirectly, cheaply, and with the Royal Air Force as the enforcer. Iraq the state was invented in those two years.
entries.note: Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007); Toby Dodge, 'Inventing Iraq' (2003).

entries.label: Faisal I and the founding of the Kingdom
entries.hint: Faisal, the Arab Revolt's field commander, arrived from Syria to be made king by a referendum that returned 96 per cent. In twelve years he negotiated a series of treaties that turned the Mandate into a nominal independence, got a constitution and a parliament, secured the oil concession and Mosul, and brought Iraq into the League as a state in 1932. He also wrote, privately, that there was 'still no Iraqi people'.
entries.note: Ali Allawi, 'Faisal I of Iraq' (2014); Faisal's 1933 memorandum quoted in Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978).

entries.label: Ghazi and the boy-king
entries.hint: Ghazi, young and nationalist, ran anti-British and pan-Arab broadcasts from a palace radio station, first raised the claim to Kuwait, and died in a car crash in 1939 that many Iraqis were sure was murder. His three-year-old son Faisal II succeeded under the regency of his uncle Abd al-Ilah, a figure so tied to Britain and the pashas that the monarchy never recovered its standing.
entries.note: Phebe Marr, 'The Modern History of Iraq' (2017); Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007).

entries.label: Nuri al-Saʿid and the old regime
entries.hint: An Ottoman officer who had joined the Arab Revolt, Nuri al-Saʿid was prime minister fourteen times over three decades and the real manager of the monarchy: pro-British, anti-communist, a master of the rigged election and the state of emergency, the architect of the Baghdad Pact. Indispensable to the palace and the British and increasingly hated in the street, he embodied the regime that fell in 1958.
entries.note: Lord Birdwood, 'Nuri as-Said: A Study in Arab Leadership' (1959); Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978).

entries.label: The army and the coups
entries.hint: In October 1936 General Bakr Sidqi marched on Baghdad and installed a government — the first military coup in the modern Arab world. It set a pattern: over the next five years there were six more coups and counter-coups, and a clique of pan-Arab colonels, the 'Golden Square', came to hold the veto over Iraqi politics. The army had learned that it could make and unmake governments, and it did not forget.
entries.note: Reeva Simon, 'Iraq Between the Two World Wars: The Militarist Origins of Tyranny' (1986).

entries.label: The Rashid Ali affair
entries.hint: In April 1941 Rashid Ali al-Gaylani and the Golden Square seized power, repudiated the British treaty, and sought Axis help. Britain reinforced from India and its base at Habbaniyya, won a thirty-day war, and put the regent back. In the two days between the collapse and the reoccupation, a mob attacked the Jewish quarter of Baghdad — the Farhud — and killed around a hundred and eighty people. It was the beginning of the end for Iraqi Jewry.
entries.note: Robert Lyman, 'Iraq 1941' (2006); the Farhud in Zvi Yehuda & Shmuel Moreh (eds.), 'Al-Farhud' (2010).

entries.label: The opposition parties
entries.hint: Against the palace and the pashas stood a spectrum: the Iraqi Communist Party, founded in 1934, strongest among the Shia poor and the minorities and the students; the National Democratic Party of the reforming middle class; the pan-Arab Istiqlal; and, from 1952, an Iraqi branch of the Baʿth. Suppressed, jailed and hanged by turns, they were the real politics of the country, and the street was theirs.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes and the Revolutionary Movements of Iraq' (1978).

entries.label: The 14 July Revolution
entries.hint: Before dawn on 14 July 1958 a brigade under Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim, one of the Free Officers, seized Baghdad. The royal family was machine-gunned in the palace courtyard; Nuri al-Saʿid, caught the next day trying to flee disguised, was shot and his body dragged through the streets. The Hashemite monarchy and the British order in Iraq ended in a morning, and were not restored.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Juan Romero, 'The Iraqi Revolution of 1958' (2011).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Mesopotamian campaign and the siege of Kut, the 1920 Revolt, the Simele massacre of the Assyrians, the Anglo-Iraqi War and the Farhud, the Barzani revolts, and the Wathba and the street risings of the 1950s

entries.label: The Mesopotamian campaign and the siege of Kut
entries.hint: After taking Basra in 1914 the Anglo-Indian force pushed up the Tigris, was checked at Ctesiphon, and fell back to Kut, where thirteen thousand men were besieged and starved into surrender in April 1916 — Britain's worst defeat of the war. A rebuilt army took Baghdad in March 1917 and grabbed Mosul as the armistice came into force. The three provinces were now under British occupation.
entries.note: Charles Townshend, 'When God Made Hell: The British Invasion of Mesopotamia 1914–1921' (2010).

entries.label: The 1920 Revolt
entries.hint: In the summer of 1920 the tribes of the mid-Euphrates rose against British rule, with a fatwa from the senior mujtahid of Karbala and the towns of Najaf and Karbala behind them. It spread across the country and took months, the RAF, and armoured columns to put down — some nine thousand Iraqi and two thousand British and Indian dead, forty million pounds spent. It forced Britain to rule through an Arab king instead, and became the founding myth of Iraqi nationalism.
entries.note: Amal Vinogradov, 'The 1920 Revolt in Iraq Reconsidered' (1972); Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007).

entries.label: The Simele massacre
entries.hint: In August 1933 the Iraqi army, part of it under Bakr Sidqi, massacred Assyrian villagers in the district of Dohuk — figures range from six hundred to three thousand — after a clash with an armed Assyrian group near the Syrian border. Baghdad greeted the returning troops as heroes. It was the first mass atrocity of the newly independent state, weeks after Faisal I's death, and a warning of what the army would do.
entries.note: Sargon Donabed, 'Reforging a Forgotten History: Iraq and the Assyrians in the Twentieth Century' (2015); Khaldun Husry, 'The Assyrian Affair of 1933' (1974).

entries.label: The Anglo-Iraqi War and the Farhud
entries.hint: The thirty-day war of 1941 — the RAF flying from the besieged base at Habbaniyya, a relief column across the desert from Palestine, the Rashid Ali government collapsing — restored the British position. In the gap between the regime's flight and the army's return, on the first two days of June, a mob and elements of the police and army attacked Baghdad's Jews. About a hundred and eighty were killed, and a community began to plan its exit.
entries.note: Robert Lyman, 'Iraq 1941' (2006); Orit Bashkin, 'New Babylonians' (2012).

entries.label: The Barzani revolts
entries.hint: The Kurdish north rose against Baghdad again and again: Ahmad Barzani in 1931–32, then his brother Mustafa in 1943–45, each crushed by the army and the RAF. Mustafa fled to the short-lived Kurdish republic at Mahabad in Iran in 1946, and when it fell walked his men to the Soviet Union, where he waited out the monarchy. The demand for Kurdish autonomy was never met, and never dropped.
entries.note: David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004); Wadie Jwaideh, 'The Kurdish National Movement' (2006).

entries.label: The Wathba and the risings of the 1950s
entries.hint: In January 1948 Baghdad rose against a new treaty with Britain signed at Portsmouth — the Wathba, the Leap — and the shooting of demonstrators on the bridges killed the treaty and shook the regime. It was the first of a decade of street risings: the 1952 Intifada, the mass protests over Suez in 1956, strikes and student demonstrations led by the communists. The palace held the army; the opposition held the street.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Eric Davis, 'Memories of State' (2005).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Mandate state and indirect rule through the RAF, the 1925 Organic Law and the managed monarchy, the oil and the state's income, the land regime and the making of the sheikhs, the army as the state's core, and the Development Board

entries.label: The Mandate state and the RAF
entries.hint: After the 1920 Revolt Britain governed on the cheap: a treaty in place of the Mandate's name, British advisers attached to every ministry, and the Royal Air Force — not an army — as the instrument of control, bombing recalcitrant tribes from the air. Even after independence in 1932 the airbases at Habbaniyya and Shaibah stayed British by treaty, and so did the real say over defence and foreign policy.
entries.note: Priya Satia, 'Spies in Arabia' (2008) and 'The Defense of Inhumanity: Air Control and the British Idea of Arabia' (2006); Peter Sluglett, 'Britain in Iraq 1914–1932' (2007).

entries.label: The Organic Law and the managed monarchy
entries.hint: The 1925 constitution gave Iraq a king, a two-chamber parliament, a cabinet and a bill of rights — a liberal shape. Underneath, the same few hundred landowning and official families held the seats, the elections were arranged by the interior ministry, and the king could dissolve the chamber at will. It was a constitutional monarchy in form and an oligarchy in fact, and the gap between the two corroded its legitimacy.
entries.note: the Iraqi Organic Law (al-Qānūn al-Asāsī) of 1925; Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978).

entries.label: The oil and the state's income
entries.hint: The Iraq Petroleum Company, an international consortium, held the concession from 1925; Kirkuk came in with a great gusher in 1927; and a 50-50 profit-sharing deal in 1952 multiplied the royalty overnight. Oil went from a minor revenue to the overwhelming one. The state began to float on it — able to spend without taxing, and so, in the long run, without needing consent.
entries.note: Marion Farouk-Sluglett & Peter Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001), on the rentier background; the IPC agreements in Marian Kent, 'Oil and Empire' (1976).

entries.label: The land regime and the making of the sheikhs
entries.hint: The monarchy completed what the Ottoman Land Code had begun. Laws of 1932 and 1938 confirmed the shaykhs' title to tribal land and bound the cultivator to it by debt; state land was granted out in vast blocks to the loyal. By 1958 a few thousand landlords held most of the country's farmland and the mass of the rural population were sharecroppers or landless. The landlord bloc was the monarchy's base in parliament.
entries.note: the Law Governing the Rights and Duties of Cultivators (1933); Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Robert Fernea, 'Shaykh and Effendi' (1970).

entries.label: The army as the core of the state
entries.hint: Conscription came in 1934, and the army grew fast — the one national institution, and the one with guns. It carried out the Simele massacre, made the coups of 1936–41, and produced from its officer schools a self-conscious political class that believed the country's problems were the politicians' fault and the soldiers' to fix. Every Iraqi regime from 1936 to 2003 would rest, in the end, on the army.
entries.note: Reeva Simon, 'Iraq Between the Two World Wars' (1986); Adeed Dawisha, 'Iraq: A Political History' (2009).

entries.label: The Development Board and the technocratic state
entries.hint: In 1950 the government set up a Development Board and gave it seventy per cent of the oil revenue to spend on dams, drainage, roads and housing, staffed with foreign engineers and planners. It was a serious attempt at planned development, and it built real things. But it worked slowly, its benefits reached the landlords before the fallahin, and a population that could see the oil money wanted results it was not getting.
entries.note: Fahim Qubain, 'The Reconstruction of Iraq 1950–1957' (1958); Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The exodus of the Jews and the end of a community of 2,500 years, the Shia clergy and the modern state, the rise of communism and Arab nationalism as the new faiths, and the Christians, Yazidis and minorities in the nationalist state

entries.label: The exodus of the Jews
entries.hint: The Farhud of 1941 was the hinge. Through the 1940s came anti-Zionist laws, dismissals, arrests and a show hanging; then in 1950–51 a law let Jews leave if they gave up their citizenship, and another froze their property. In Operation Ezra and Nehemiah about a hundred and twenty-five thousand — nearly the whole community — were airlifted to Israel. A Jewish presence in Iraq going back to the Babylonian Exile was over in a decade.
entries.note: Orit Bashkin, 'New Babylonians: A History of Jews in Modern Iraq' (2012); Moshe Gat, 'The Jewish Exodus from Iraq 1948–1951' (1997).

entries.label: The Shia clergy and the modern state
entries.hint: The marjaʿiyya that had led the 1920 Revolt largely withdrew from politics afterward. Britain deported Iranian mujtahids, the modern state stripped the shrine cities of their autonomy, and the senior scholars — Muhsin al-Hakim above all — turned to a cautious quietism, husbanding the seminary and staying out of the government's way. The clergy's political silence in these decades is as significant as its later noise.
entries.note: Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994); Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003).

entries.label: Communism and Arab nationalism
entries.hint: For the educated young, ideology replaced religion as the language of politics. The Iraqi Communist Party drew the Shia poor, the slum-dwellers and the minorities with a promise of land and equality; Arab nationalism drew the Sunni officers and students with a dream of unity and dignity. Both despised the monarchy. The contest between these two secular faiths would run through Iraqi history for the next half-century.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Eric Davis, 'Memories of State: Politics, History, and Collective Identity in Modern Iraq' (2005).

entries.label: The Christians, Yazidis and minorities in the nationalist state
entries.hint: After Simele the Assyrians scattered — many to a strip of villages on the Khabur in Syria — and the Chaldean Catholic Church became the main body of Iraqi Christians. Armenian survivors of the genocide had settled in the towns; the Yazidis of Sinjar and the Mandaeans of the rivers held on. All of them found that the Arab-nationalist state had less room for a minority than the Ottoman one had, and watched the fate of the Jews with alarm.
entries.note: Sargon Donabed, 'Reforging a Forgotten History' (2015); Nelida Fuccaro, 'The Other Kurds: Yazidis in Colonial Iraq' (1999).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The free-verse revolution of 1947 and the making of the modern Arabic poem, Jewad Selim and modern Iraqi art, the Baghdad of the architects, the press and radio and the effendiyya, and the archaeologists and the national past

entries.label: The free-verse revolution
entries.hint: In 1947 two young Baghdad poets, Badr Shakir al-Sayyab and Nazik al-Malaʾika, published poems that broke the fixed metre and rhyme that Arabic verse had kept for fourteen centuries, writing in irregular lines built on a single foot. Al-Sayyab's 'Rain Song' fused the new form with Iraqi imagery and political grief. It was the founding act of modern Arabic poetry, and it happened in Iraq.
entries.note: Salma Khadra Jayyusi, 'Trends and Movements in Modern Arabic Poetry' (1977); Nazik al-Malaʾika, 'Qaḍāyā al-Shiʿr al-Muʿāṣir' (1962).

entries.label: Jewad Selim and modern Iraqi art
entries.hint: The Baghdad Group for Modern Art, founded in 1951 around the sculptor Jewad Selim, set out to make a modern art rooted in Mesopotamian and Islamic heritage — 'seeking inspiration from tradition'. Selim's designs for the Monument of Freedom, a frieze of the 1958 revolution reading like an Assyrian relief, became the founding work of the national art and still stands over Tahrir Square.
entries.note: Nada Shabout, 'Modern Arab Art: Formation of Arab Aesthetics' (2007); Zainab Bahrani & others on Jewad Selim.

entries.label: The Baghdad of the architects
entries.hint: Flush with oil money, the Development Board commissioned the age's greatest architects to design a modern capital: Frank Lloyd Wright drew an opera house and a plan for 'Greater Baghdad', Le Corbusier a sports complex, Gropius and his firm the university, Alvar Aalto a museum, Doxiadis the housing. Most of it was unbuilt or half-built when the monarchy fell, but the ambition marked Baghdad as a city that briefly stood at the centre of modern architecture.
entries.note: Caecilia Pieri, 'Baghdad: The City in Its Prime' (2015); Panayiota Pyla & others on the Development Board commissions.

entries.label: The press, the radio and the effendiyya
entries.hint: Politics ran on print and talk: dozens of newspapers, the palace and then the state radio, the coffee-house argument and the party cell. The audience and the actors were the effendiyya — the salaried, school-educated, town-dwelling class of clerks, teachers, officers and students that the Ottoman and then the monarchy's schools had created, and that the regime could neither satisfy nor control.
entries.note: Orit Bashkin, 'The Other Iraq: Pluralism and Culture in Hashemite Iraq' (2009); Michael Eppel, 'The Elite, the Effendiyya, and the Growth of Nationalism' (1998).

entries.label: The archaeologists and the national heritage
entries.hint: Gertrude Bell drew up the first Antiquities Law and founded the Iraq Museum in 1926, taking half the finds from each dig. The great excavations ran on — Woolley's Ur with its royal tombs, the German return to Uruk, Mallowan at Nimrud — and a 1936 law finally stopped the export of finds. An Iraqi archaeology, and a state that claimed the Sumerians and Assyrians as its own ancestors, began here.
entries.note: Magnus Bernhardsson, 'Reclaiming a Plundered Past: Archaeology and Nation Building in Modern Iraq' (2005).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The intellectual project of making a nation from three vilayets, Marxism and the ICP's thinkers, Ali al-Wardi and the sociology of Iraq, and the revival of religious thought at Najaf

entries.label: Making a nation from three vilayets
entries.hint: The monarchy's central intellectual task was to persuade Sunni Arabs, Shia Arabs, Kurds, Turkmen, Christians and Jews that they were one people. Satiʿ al-Husri, running the education ministry, built a school curriculum around Arab nationalism; others argued for an Iraqi territorial patriotism that could include the non-Arabs. The two answers — Arabism and Iraqi wataniyya — were never reconciled, and the question is still open.
entries.note: William Cleveland, 'The Making of an Arab Nationalist: Sātiʿ al-Ḥuṣrī' (1971); Eric Davis, 'Memories of State' (2005).

entries.label: Marxism and the ICP's thinkers
entries.hint: The Communist Party did the period's most serious analysis of Iraqi society — its 'semi-feudal, semi-colonial' model of the landlords, the oil companies and the British, and its programme of land reform and independence. Its founder-organiser Fahd built a disciplined underground that outlasted him; he and two comrades were hanged in the public squares in 1949, and the party only grew.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes and the Revolutionary Movements of Iraq' (1978), the fullest account.

entries.label: Ali al-Wardi and the sociology of Iraq
entries.hint: The sociologist Ali al-Wardi turned an analytic eye on his own society: the tension between the Bedouin values of the countryside and the settled values of the town, the 'split personality' he thought that tension bred in the Iraqi, the workings of the tribes and the sects. His books, popular and controversial, were the beginning of an Iraqi social science and are still argued over.
entries.note: ʿAli al-Wardi, 'Shakhṣiyyat al-Fard al-ʿIrāqī' (1951) and 'Dirāsa fī Ṭabīʿat al-Mujtamaʿ al-ʿIrāqī' (1965).

entries.label: The revival of religious thought at Najaf
entries.hint: As communism swept the Shia young, a circle of scholars at Najaf around the young Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr began to work out a modern Islamic answer — a political theory and an economics that could compete with Marxism on its own ground. The books would come in the early 1960s and the party, al-Daʿwa, would form around them; but the milieu that produced Iraq's Islamist movement was taking shape in the last years of the monarchy.
entries.note: Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003); Chibli Mallat, 'The Renewal of Islamic Law: Muhammad Baqer as-Sadr' (1993).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The oil economy takes hold, the land question and rural misery, the shurūq migration and the sarīfa slums, the Development Board and the dams, and the modern sector and the middle class

entries.label: The oil economy takes hold
entries.hint: Kirkuk's first well blew out of control in 1927 and burned for days. Pipelines carried the crude across the desert to the Mediterranean; a 50-50 agreement in 1952 raised the state's take fivefold in a year. By the mid-1950s oil paid for most of the government and all of the Development Board. Iraq had become an oil state — its politics increasingly about who controlled the flow of money, not the work of the people.
entries.note: Marian Kent, 'Oil and Empire' (1976); Marion Farouk-Sluglett & Peter Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001), on the rentier economy.

entries.label: The land question and rural misery
entries.hint: By the 1950s a few thousand families held most of Iraq's farmland and roughly two-thirds of rural people were landless or near it. The sharecropper's share of the crop kept falling, the debt kept rising, the diet and the health were among the worst in the region, and the southern rural economy was collapsing. The land question was the great unsolved problem of the monarchy, and it fed the revolution that ended it.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Doreen Warriner, 'Land Reform and Development in the Middle East' (1957).

entries.label: The shuruq and the sarifa slums
entries.hint: Fleeing the debt and the estates of the south, hundreds of thousands of dispossessed peasants — the shurūq, the easterners — drifted to Baghdad and built shantytowns of reed huts, the sarīfa, on the city's edge. By 1958 perhaps a third of the capital lived in them, without water, drains or work. They were the recruiting ground of the Communist Party, and a generation later of the Sadrist movement.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978); Doris Phillips, 'Rural-to-Urban Migration in Iraq' (1959).

entries.label: The Development Board and the dams
entries.hint: The Development Board's engineers built the Wadi Tharthar and Habbaniyya flood escapes that finally protected Baghdad from the Tigris, the Dokan and Derbendi Khan dams on the tributaries, the Samarra Barrage, and drainage and irrigation schemes across the country. It was a real programme, and after four thousand years it began to give Iraq control of its rivers. It was also too slow for the moment, and it fell with the regime.
entries.note: Fahim Qubain, 'The Reconstruction of Iraq 1950–1957' (1958).

entries.label: The middle class and the modern economy
entries.hint: Alongside the rural collapse, an urban modern economy grew: government jobs, the professions, banking, small industry, trade, the cinema. Much of the commerce had been in Jewish, Christian and Armenian hands, and the departure of the Jews after 1951 hollowed it out. A salaried middle class of officials, teachers and officers expanded — educated, frustrated, and, by 1958, mostly against the regime that had made it.
entries.note: Charles Issawi, 'The Economic History of the Middle East 1800–1914' background; Phebe Marr, 'The Modern History of Iraq' (2017).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Air power as the instrument of rule, the dams and the rivers tamed at last, the oil infrastructure across the desert, and the railway, the road and the car knitting the country together

entries.label: Air control and the aeroplane
entries.hint: Iraq was the first place the Royal Air Force ran a colony from the air: squadrons based at Hinaidi and Habbaniyya policed the country by bombing villages and flocks that would not pay tax or hand over rebels. It was cheap, and it worked, and its architects — Trenchard, then Harris — carried the method and the mentality on to bigger wars. The Iraqi air force that grew up beside it inherited the same logic.
entries.note: Priya Satia, 'The Defense of Inhumanity: Air Control and the British Idea of Arabia' (2006); David Omissi, 'Air Power and Colonial Control' (1990).

entries.label: The rivers tamed at last
entries.hint: The 1954 flood came within a metre of drowning Baghdad and spurred the Development Board to finish the flood-control works: the Tharthar scheme diverting the Tigris surplus into a desert lake, the Habbaniyya escape doing the same for the Euphrates, the Dokan and Derbendi Khan dams holding back the mountain torrents. For the first time since Sasanian days, the two rivers were substantially under control.
entries.note: Fahim Qubain, 'The Reconstruction of Iraq' (1958); the Iraqi hydrological engineering literature on the Tharthar.

entries.label: The oil infrastructure
entries.hint: The Iraq Petroleum Company built a vast industrial system almost entirely outside Iraqi control: the Kirkuk field, the pumping stations, the twin pipelines running seven hundred kilometres across the desert to Haifa and Tripoli, and finally the Daura refinery near Baghdad in 1955. Iraqis worked it as labourers and clerks; the engineering, the pricing and the profits were the consortium's.
entries.note: Marian Kent, 'Oil and Empire' (1976); the IPC company records.

entries.label: The railway, the road and the car
entries.hint: The British completed the north–south railway and joined it to the Turkish line; roads spread; car and bus ownership climbed; Iraqi Airways began flying in 1945. For the first time the country was physically knitted together — Basra to Mosul in a day, the villages reachable — which made both a national economy and a centralised state possible in a way they had never been before.
entries.note: Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007); the Iraqi State Railways histories.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Iraq in the British imperial system, the Palestine question and Arab politics, the Baghdad Pact and the Cold War, the oil consortium and the world market, and the Kurdish question across four borders

entries.label: Iraq in the British system
entries.hint: Independent in name from 1932, Iraq stayed inside Britain's imperial arrangements until 1958: the treaties, the two airbases, the say over defence and oil, the sterling balances, the reoccupation in 1941. Britain's man Nuri al-Saʿid ran the government; Britain's interests set the limits. The resentment of that tie — visible in every street rising — was one of the strongest forces in Iraqi politics, and it brought the regime down.
entries.note: Peter Sluglett, 'Britain in Iraq: Contriving King and Country' (2007); Daniel Silverfarb, 'Britain's Informal Empire in the Middle East' (1986).

entries.label: The Palestine question and the 1948 war
entries.hint: Iraq sent volunteers to the 1936 Palestine revolt and an army brigade to the 1948 war, whose defeat was a national humiliation blamed on the old regime. The war fed an anti-Zionist fury that engulfed Iraq's own Jews, and it made the Palestinian cause a permanent fixture of Iraqi politics — a stick to beat any government seen as soft on Israel or close to the West.
entries.note: Michael Eppel, 'The Palestine Conflict in the History of Modern Iraq' (1994).

entries.label: The Baghdad Pact and the isolation of the monarchy
entries.hint: In 1955 Nuri al-Saʿid brought Iraq into a Western-sponsored alliance with Turkey, Britain, Pakistan and Iran — the Baghdad Pact. It was meant to hold the northern tier against the Soviet Union. In fact it isolated the monarchy: Nasser's Egypt denounced it as imperialism, the Arab street agreed, and the pact became a symbol of everything the opposition hated about the regime. The revolution took Iraq straight out of it.
entries.note: Elie Podeh, 'The Quest for Hegemony in the Arab World: The Struggle over the Baghdad Pact' (1995).

entries.label: The consortium and the world market
entries.hint: The Iraq Petroleum Company was owned by the majors — BP, Shell, the French CFP, and two American firms — under a 'Red Line' agreement that bound them not to compete separately in the old Ottoman lands. They held Iraqi output below its potential to protect prices elsewhere, and set the posted price themselves. The friction over control and revenue would push Iraq to help found OPEC in Baghdad in 1960 and to nationalise the company in 1972.
entries.note: Daniel Yergin, 'The Prize' (1991); Marian Kent, 'Oil and Empire' (1976).

entries.label: The Kurdish question across the borders
entries.hint: The Kurds ended up split among Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Syria by the post-war settlement, and their politics ran across all four frontiers. When a Kurdish republic rose briefly at Mahabad in Iran in 1946, Iraqi Kurds under Mustafa Barzani fought for it; when it fell he walked his fighters to the Soviet Union and waited. The status of the Kurds inside Iraq was left unsettled by the monarchy, as it would be by every regime after.
entries.note: David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004); William Eagleton, 'The Kurdish Republic of 1946' (1963).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The invented state whose legitimacy was contested from birth, the beginning of the oil curse, the failed liberal experiment, and the 14 July watershed

entries.label: The state contested from birth
entries.hint: Iraq was assembled by Britain from three Ottoman provinces around an imported king, its borders drawn for imperial convenience, its army and administration staffed from a Sunni-Arab minority ruling a Shia-Arab and Kurdish majority. Its legitimacy was disputed from the first day — by the tribes of 1920, by the Kurds, by the Shia clergy, by the nationalists — and the state has spent a century unable to settle the argument about who it belongs to.
entries.note: Toby Dodge, 'Inventing Iraq: The Failure of Nation Building and a History Denied' (2003); Adeed Dawisha, 'Iraq: A Political History' (2009).

entries.label: The oil curse begins
entries.hint: Oil revenue created a state that floated above its own society — one that could pay its bills without taxing its people, and so did not have to answer to them; one whose seizure was the only prize in politics that mattered. The rentier pattern that took hold under the monarchy would deform Iraqi political life through the republic, the Baʿth and the decades after 2003.
entries.note: Kiren Aziz Chaudhry, 'The Price of Wealth' (1997); Marion Farouk-Sluglett & Peter Sluglett, 'Iraq Since 1958' (2001).

entries.label: The failed liberal experiment
entries.hint: For a generation Iraq had the outward forms of liberal politics — a constitution, a parliament, an argumentative press, parties. It failed because the substance was missing: the elections were fixed, the land regime locked the countryside out, the British tie discredited every government, and the army held the final card. By 1958 the liberal monarchy had no defenders, and what replaced it was harder.
entries.note: Charles Tripp, 'A History of Iraq' (2007); Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978).

entries.label: The 14 July watershed
entries.hint: The revolution of 1958 ended the monarchy, the British order and the landlord parliament in a single morning, and opened the republican Iraq of coups, radicalism and, in time, the Baʿth. It was a genuine liberation from a discredited regime, and it was also the point after which Iraqi politics turned violent and stayed that way. Almost nothing from before 1958 was ever restored.
entries.note: Robert McNamara & others (eds.), 'The 1958 Iraqi Revolution' background; Juan Romero, 'The Iraqi Revolution of 1958' (2011).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Faisal I, Nuri al-Saʿid, Gertrude Bell, Badr Shakir al-Sayyab, and the shaykh turned pump-landlord of Amara

entries.label: Faisal I
entries.hint: A Hashemite prince from the Hejaz, the Arab Revolt's field commander, thrown off the Syrian throne by the French and handed the Iraqi one by the British — a king of a country he had never seen. He worked hard to make an Iraqi nation and a real independence, and won a version of both by 1932. He died in 1933 exhausted and pessimistic, writing that the people he ruled were 'unimaginable masses' with nothing in common, and leaving a fragile state to a boy.
entries.note: Ali A. Allawi, 'Faisal I of Iraq' (2014).

entries.label: Nuri al-Saʿid
entries.hint: An Ottoman staff officer who joined the Arab Revolt and then spent thirty years as the monarchy's indispensable man — fourteen times prime minister, master of the security file and the fixed election, the author of the Baghdad Pact, the friend of every British ambassador. On the day after the revolution he was caught in the street disguised in a woman's cloak, shot, and his body dragged behind a car and burned. The manner of it measured the hatred the old regime had earned.
entries.note: Waldemar Gallman, 'Iraq under General Nuri' (1964); Hanna Batatu, 'The Old Social Classes' (1978).

entries.label: Gertrude Bell
entries.hint: The British traveller, Arabist and intelligence officer who sat at the Cairo Conference table, argued for Faisal, helped fix the frontiers, and then — with the political work done — wrote the Antiquities Law and founded the Iraq Museum, of which she was the first director. She died in Baghdad in 1926, of an overdose, and is buried there. She is the type of the imperial expert as maker of a nation, and of its museum.
entries.note: Georgina Howell, 'Gertrude Bell: Queen of the Desert, Shaper of Nations' (2006); Magnus Bernhardsson, 'Reclaiming a Plundered Past' (2005).

entries.label: Badr Shakir al-Sayyab
entries.hint: A poet from a poor village near Basra, briefly a communist, later hunted for it, who with Nazik al-Malaʾika broke the classical Arabic line in 1947 and, in poems like 'Rain Song' and 'The River and Death', bound the new free verse to Iraqi place and grief. He died of a wasting disease in a Kuwait hospital in 1964, thirty-eight years old and nearly destitute — the age's artistic conscience, and its emblematic wasted life.
entries.note: Terri DeYoung, 'Placing the Poet: Badr Shakir al-Sayyab and Postcolonial Iraq' (1998).

entries.label: The pump-landlord of Amara
entries.hint: A tribal shaykh of the Bani Lam or the Al bu Muhammad who turned the state's land grants into tens of thousands of acres, put diesel pumps on the riverbank, and ran an estate of debt-bound sharecroppers he could evict at will. He sat in the Senate, dined at the palace, and watched the men who fled his fields swell the reed-hut slums of Baghdad — the slums whose anger would help destroy the order that had made him rich.
entries.note: Robert Fernea, 'Shaykh and Effendi: Changing Patterns of Authority Among the El Shabana of Southern Iraq' (1970); Hanna Batatu (1978).
